title: Cotton crosses the ocean
hook: How can a fragment in Egypt reveal an Indian Ocean connection?

knows: Events happen in places and at different times.

objective: The route is reconstructed from objects and records, not a surviving ship’s track.

claims.text: Medieval: Production. Gujarat produces dyed and printed cottons.
claims.source: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/red-sea-textile-trade — Production, Genizah documents, Fustat fragments and 1920s–1930s excavations

claims.text: 10th–13th c.: Exchange. Genizah records document Gujarat–Egypt trade.
claims.source: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/red-sea-textile-trade — Production, Genizah documents, Fustat fragments and 1920s–1930s excavations

claims.text: 13th–14th c.: Use and discard. Indian textiles survive around Fustat.
claims.source: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/red-sea-textile-trade — Production, Genizah documents, Fustat fragments and 1920s–1930s excavations

claims.text: 1920s–30s: Rediscovery. Excavations reveal fragments in Egypt.
claims.source: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/red-sea-textile-trade — Production, Genizah documents, Fustat fragments and 1920s–1930s excavations

claims.text: The route is reconstructed from objects and records, not a surviving ship’s track. Gujarati cottons reached Egypt through Indian Ocean and Red Sea connections. Fragments preserved in Egypt’s dry conditions, together with Genizah documents, reveal exchange that a political-border map would miss.
claims.source: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/red-sea-textile-trade — Production, Genizah documents, Fustat fragments and 1920s–1930s excavations

claims.text: Exact excavation sites for the Met fragments are unknown; sea links are generalized.
